### Generation of Tph1-bacTRAP mice

A C57BL/6 BAC genomic clone RP23–4G4, which contains the locus of Tph1 gene, was isolated from a RP23 mouse genomic BAC library (http://www.gensat.org/). BAC transgenic mice were produced according to published protocols (Gong et al., 2003). The shuttle vector (S296-1) was digested with AscI and NotI. A 420-bp ‘A box’ fragment direct upstream of the ATG start codon of the Tph1 gene was designed to be used for homologous recombination, amplified, digested with AscI and NotI and cloned into the shuttle vector containing EGFP-RPL12. After electroporation, co-integration was identified by ampicillin resistance and verified by Southern blot using the A box sequence as the probe target. The modified BAC DNA was injected into fertilized oocytes of C57B6/J to generate the Tph1-bacTRAP line.

### Tissue dissociation and flow cytometry

Male mice aged 8–12 weeks were used. After the animals were sacrificed, small intestine and colon were surgically removed, rinsed with ice-cold PBS and the luminal contents flushed out with PBS using a 20-ml syringe with an 18-gauge round-tip feeding needle (Roboz Surgical Instrument, FN-7906). Duodenal and jejunal tissue was dissected between 1–5 and 13–17 cm distal of pyloric constriction. Ileum was dissected between 1 and 9 cm rostral of ileocecal junction. For the colon, the distal 4 cm tissue of descending colon was dissected as distal colon and the segment with banded lining distal to cecum was dissected as proximal colon. Dissected gut segments were inverted inside out and incubated in DMEM supplemented with 3 mM DTT (Sigma Life Science, D9779), 1 mM EDTA (Gibco, 15575-038) and 10% FBS (Gibco, 26410-079) at 37°C for 30 min with consistent rotation. The released epithelial tissue was cut into smaller pieces, triturated with a 1000-µl pipette and dissociated in a collagenase solution with 1 U of Dispase (Stem Cell Technologies, 07923), 2 mg/ml Collagenase IV (Worthington Biochemical Corporation, LS004186), and 100 U DNase I (Worthington Biochemical Corporation, LS006330) in DMEM/F12 medium for 20–30 min at 37°C with gentle mixing every 10 min. The dissociated cells were washed and filtered through a 100-µm cell strainer followed by a 40-µm cell strainer. The flow-through was spun down and filtered through another 40-µm cell strainer. The viability of the single-cell suspension was determined using trypan blue staining.

Cell pellets from the single-cell suspension were resuspended in FACS buffer (PBS, 5% FBS, and 5 mM EDTA) for staining in ice for 10 min with 7-AAD (BD Biosciences, #51-68981E). Only 7-AAD− cells were considered as viable cells. To obtain cells for scRNA-seq, GFP+/7-AAD− and GFP−/7-AAD− cells were collected from the Tph1-bacTRAP mice, while tdTomato+/7-AAD− and tdTomato−/7-AAD− cells are collected from the Neurod1-tdTomato mice. Single-cell suspensions from different segments of gut were prepared and sorted separately. Single-cell suspensions from duodenum and jejunum were prepared from a single animal, while segments of proximal colon and distal colon were pooled from two and eight animals, respectively, to acquire sufficient numbers of cells. For ileum, however, even pooling eight animals did not yield adequate number for unbiased analysis (intestinal stem cells and TACs were disproportionally enriched in the GFP+ cells, see data analysis), thus ileum was excluded from the subsequent scRNA-seq analysis.

### Library preparation and sequencing

Single-cell suspensions of freshly sorted cells were spun down to concentrate and were counted. All scRNA-seq libraries were prepared in parallel using Chromium Single Cell 3′Reagent Kits (10X Genomics; Pleasanton, CA, USA; Tph1-bacTRAP and small intestine of Neurod1-tdTomato: v2; colon of Neurod1-tdTomato: v3) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Generated libraries were sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq4000 instrument, followed by de-multiplexing and mapping to the mouse genome (build mm10) using CellRanger (10X Genomics, version 2.1.1). Our sequencing saturation ranged between 61.0 and 81.7%.

### Multiplex fluorescent single-molecule RNA in situ hybridization (smRNA-FISH)

To prepare tissue sections for RNA-FISH, wild-type C57BL/6 mice (8–10 weeks) were sacrificed, intestine and colon were dissected as described above, cleaned and fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (Electron Microscopy Sciences, 15713) at 4°C overnight, and cryoprotected in 30% sucrose (Ward’s Science, 57-50-1) for 24 hr before being embedded in 100% O.C.T. compound (Tissue-Tek). Cryosections were prepared at 12 µm. Single-molecule RNA-FISH was performed using the RNAscope. Multiplex Fluorescent Detection Kit v2 (323100, Advanced Cell Diagnostics) according to the manufacturer’s instructions using TSA with Cy3, Cy5, and/or Fluorescein (Perkin Elmer NEL760001KT). All sections were counterstained with DAPI (1:1000; Invitrogen D1306). All co-staining was performed on tissue samples from at least three mice. Images were acquired on Zeiss LSM780 confocal microscope. Subsequent processing of images was performed in Fiji (Schindelin et al., 2012; Rueden et al., 2017), including channel merging, pseudocoloring, maximum intensity projection, and brightness adjustment.

### Quantification of smRNA-FISH

To quantitate crypt–villus distribution of cells, 9 × 9 tile images (1024-pixel × 1024-pixel) of an entire cross section of duodenum were acquired on Zeiss LSM780 and stitched in ZEN software. For automated analysis, images were preprocessed in Fiji (2.0.0) by maximum intensity projection, background subtraction and contrast enhancement, and the processed images were output as binary images for each channel. A custom CellProfiler pipeline was built to quantitate co-staining of two or three channels. Briefly, regions of interest (ROIs) were manually drawn on the DAPI channel in order to count cells separately in the crypts versus the villi. For each set of images, objects were identified independent in each channel, the signal of which was expanded by a 5-pixel diameter circle. If the circular objects identified from different channels overlapped, the cells were identified as double- or triple-positive. For each experiment, the pipeline was automated through images collected from at least 3 sections per animal in three animals. The number of double-positive cells (e.g., Tph1+/Cartpt+) was divided by single-positive cells (e.g., Tph1+) in each ROI and summarized across three animals to calculate mean and SEM statistics were performed using an unpaired Student’s t-test to compare enrichment in the crypts versus in the villi. To quantitate co-expression of two or three feature genes, the same pipeline was employed without demarcation of crypts versus villi.

### Quantification of Piezo2 depletion via smRNA-FISH

Sections were prepared from distal colon of either Piezo2-DTR or WT mice after intraluminal treatment of DT for 5 days. A custom CellProfiler pipeline was built to quantitate staining of Tph1 and Piezo2 channels. For each set of images, puncta (objects) were identified in the Tph1 or Piezo2 channel independently. When objects identified from the two channels overlapped, the puncta were identified as double positive; otherwise, the puncta were identified as single positive. The intensity of the Piezo2 signals was quantitated by the size of puncta. Data were summarized from four pairs of animals with two tiled images from each animal. smRNA-FISH probes are listed in Appendix 1—key resources table.

### qPCR analysis

Cells were dissociated from the stripped epithelial layer in the duodenum, jejunum, and proximal and distal colon of the Tph1-bacTRAP animals. Total RNA was prepared from the sorted regional GFP− and GFP+ cells using the RNeasy Micro Kit (QIAGEN). First-strand cDNA was synthetized from 100 ng RNA using the SuperScript III First-Strand Synthesis System (Thermo Fisher, 18080051). Quantitative PCR was performed using FastStart Universal SYBR Green Master Mix (Sigma, 4913850001). The aggregates of three housekeeping genes (B2m, Gapdh, and Rpl13a) were used to compute deltaCt. Relative gene expression was calculated by normalization against GFP− cells extracted from the duodenum. Oligonucleotide sequences are listed in Appendix 1—key resources table.

### Tissue processing for immunohistochemistry

Duodenal (descending duodenum), jejunal (segment distal to root of mesentery), proximal colon (segment with banded lining distal to cecum), and distal colon (straight descending colon) tissue were isolated from three 2-month wild-type C57Bl/6 male mice and three 8-month-old female Tph1-bacTRAP mice. The segments were opened along the mesenteric attachment, pinned onto balsa wood with the mucosal side facing up, and then fixed overnight in fixative (2% (vol/vol) formaldehyde plus 0.2% (vol/vol) picric acid in 0.1 M sodium phosphate buffer, pH 7.2) at 4°C. Following fixation, tissue was washed three times in dimethyl sulfoxide, 10 min each, followed by three washes in PBS, 10 min each. Tissue was stored in PBS containing 0.1% (vol/vol) sodium azide until ready for use. Tissue was prepared for processing by placing segments in 50% (vol/vol) PBS-sucrose-azide and 50% (vol/vol) O.C.T. mixture for 24 hr before being embedded in 100% O.C.T. compound.

### Immunohistochemistry and image analysis

Sections (12 μm) were cut and allowed to dry at room temperature for 1 hr on microscope slides (SuperFrostPlus; Menzel-Glaser; Thermo Fisher, Victoria, Australia). Sections were next incubated with 10% (vol/vol) normal horse serum prepared in PBS containing 1% (vol/vol) Triton X-100 for 30 min, followed by overnight incubation at 4°C with primary antibodies (see Appendix 1—key resources table). Sections were washed three times in PBS and incubated with secondary antibodies (see Appendix 1—key resources table) for 1 hr at room temperature. Following three washes with distilled water, sections were stained with Hoechst 33258 solution (10 µg/ml in distilled water) for 5 min to allow visualization of nuclei. Slides were washed with distilled water and coverslipped using non-fluorescent mounting medium (Dako, Carpinteria, CA, USA). Slides were allowed to dry overnight at room temperature after which they were imaged at ×40 magnification using the AxioImager microscope (Zeiss, Sydney, Australia), or with the LSM800 (Zeiss) at ×20 magnification. Immunoreactive cells were quantified by counting approximately 100 cells from each region of the gut for each of the three animals.

### Serotonin measurements

Blood samples were collected retro-orbitally from indicated animal cohorts. Animals subjected to blood collection were not used for in vivo motility assays. Serum was separated after coagulation at room temperature for 60 min, meaning that platelets could be contributing to the serotonin levels measured. Serotonin levels were detected in sera by ELISA according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Eagle Biosciences). To examine tissue serotonin levels from epithelial tissue, epithelium was extracted by incubation in DMEM supplemented with 3 mM DTT (Sigma Life Science, D9779), 1 mM EDTA (Gibco, 15575-038) and 10% FBS (Gibco, 26410-079) at 37°C for 30 min with consistent rotation. Dissociated epithelial cells were lysed with standard buffer provided in ELISA kits. Cleared supernatant was used for ELISA. For the serotonin secretion assay, ~1000 sorted cells were equilibrated in standard buffer (+0.1% wt/vol ascorbic acid) for 30 min after wash with PBS. Cells were then incubated with standard buffer supplemented with indicated drugs or vehicle control, as well as 0.1% ascorbic acid for 15 min. Supernatant and cell lysates were prepared to measure secreted serotonin and cell lysate serotonin separately, the sum of which is calculated as total serotonin level. Secreted serotonin was considered as supernatant serotonin ÷ total serotonin × 100%.

### CNO and DT administration

CNO (Tocris, 4936) was dissolved in sterile 0.9% saline (Quality Biological, 114-055-101). On the day of experiment, the animals were anesthetized with isoflurane (5%, 1 l/min). CNO at indicated doses or saline control were administrated intracolonically using a 1-ml syringe with a 22-gauge round-tip feeding needle (round tip diameter 1.25 mm, length 36 mm; Roboz Surgical Instrument, FN-7920). Initially, two different doses (60 ng/kg, 120 ng/kg) of CNO were tested. As they were equally potent to induce serum serotonin elevation, the lesser dose (60 ng/kg in 50 µl) was chosen for the rest of experiments. DT (Sigma, D0564) was reconstituted in sterile water and administrated to anesthetized animals in the same manner as CNO, at 50 µg/kg in 50 µl twice a day for 5 consecutive days. Different regimens of DT administration were tested initially to obtain the maximal depletion of Piezo2+ cells in the distal colon.

### In vivo motility assays

Animals were assigned to a random number before functional assays and data were collected in a blinded manner.

### Fecal pellet assay

The night before the assay, all animals (8–10 weeks, male) were housed singly in regular cages with wire mesh bottoms and bedding underneath with free access to food and water. After overnight acclimatization, each animal was placed into new wire mesh bottom cages. Fecal pellets were collected over 2 hr and counted for each animal. For the cohorts receiving CNO treatment, since increased fecal pellets were already observed within the first 15 min after CNO administration in the Piezo2-CHRM3* mice, we have shortened the collection time window to 15 min for this experiment.

### Bead expulsion assay

All animals (8–10 weeks male or as indicated in the manuscript) were fasted for 2 hr before assay. Briefly, the animals were anesthetized with isoflurane (5%, 1 l/min). A glass bead (2 mm in diameter, Sigma 1040140500) was placed into the colon using a disposable feeding needle with silicone tip (Fisherbrand, 01-208-89) to a distance of 2 cm from the anal verge. Mice were returned to their individual cages and allow to come back to full consciousness. Time required to expel the glass bead was monitored and recorded in each animal. The experiment was terminated at 60 min after mice became fully conscious. The mice failed to expel glass beads within this time window were reported as 60 min.

### Gastric emptying and SIT analysis

All animals (8–10 weeks, male) were fasted overnight in cages that lacked bedding. Water was withdrawn 3 hr before the experiment. Mice were orally gavaged with 100 µl sterile solution of 10 mg/ml rhodamine B dextran (Sigma R9379) in 2% methylcellulose (Sigma, M7027) through a 20-gauge round-tip feeding needle (Roboz Surgical Instrument, FN-7903). Animals were scarified 15 min after gavage; the stomach, small intestine, cecum, and colon were collected PBS. The small intestine was divided into 10 segments of equal length, and the colon (used to obtain total recovered rhodamine B fluorescence) was divided in half. Each piece of tissue was homogenized in PBS and centrifuged (2000 × g) to obtain a clear supernatant. Rhodamine fluorescence was measured in 250 µl aliquots of the supernatant (Tecan Trading, Infinite M200). Gastric empty rate was calculated as [(total recovered fluorescence − fluorescence remaining in the stomach) ÷ (total recovered fluorescence)] × 100%. Small intestinal transit was estimated by the position of the geometric center of the rhodamine B dextran in the small bowel (Miller et al., 1981). For each segment of the small intestine (1–10), the geometric center (a) was calculated as follows: a = (fluorescence in each segment × number of the segment) ÷ (total fluorescence recovered in the small intestine). The total geometric center is Σ (a of each segment). Total geometric center values are distributed between 1 (minimal motility) and 10 (maximal motility).

### Total gastrointestinal transit time analysis

Male animals between 8 and 16 weeks were used, or as indicated in the manuscript when both female and male animals were examined. The night before the experiment, animals were transferred to individual housing with free access to water only. On the day of experiment, animals had free access to food and water for 1 hr. A solution of 6% carmine red (300 µl, Sigma, C1022) was prepared using 0.5% methylcellulose (Sigma, M7027) and was administered by gavage through a 21-gauge round-tip feeding needle (Roboz Surgical Instrument, FN-7903). 90 min after gavage, fecal pellets were monitored for the presence of carmine red. Total GI transit time was calculated from the time of administration to the first observance of carmine red in stool.

### In vivo transit analysis

Male animals between 8 and 16 weeks were used for this assay. Animals were fasted overnight and then had free access to food and water for 1 hr. 100 µl Gastrosense 750 (Perkin Elmer) prepared in PBS was administered to the stomach via gavage. To assess partial intestinal transit, the GI tract (stomach to terminal colon) was removed at indicated time. Fluorescence images were obtained of the GI tract using an IVIS Lumina II In Vivo Imaging System (Perkin Elmer).

### scRNA-seq data processing

#### Gene expression matrices

Gene expression matrices were generated using the CellRanger software (10X Genomics). Sample data were aggregated using CellRanger (cellranger -aggr) and resulting data were processed further in Python (version 3.6.2) or scanpy (version 2.1.4) (Wolf et al., 2018).

#### Quality control

The following quality control steps were performed: (1) non-coding gene and genes expressed in fewer than 10 cells were not considered; (2) cells that expressed fewer than 500 genes were excluded from further analysis (suggesting a low quality of cells); (3) cells in which >10% of unique molecular identifiers (UMIs) were derived from the mitochondrial genome were removed.

#### Cell doublet removal

Since we kept our capture rate low (~2000 cells per sample) during library preparation, the cell doublet rate was low as expected. We removed potential cell doublets based on: (1) the presence of gene signatures from two different cell classes, such as epithelial markers and immune cell markers; (2) the observation of a second peak of total UMIs distribution in comparison to the cells from the same class.

#### Normalization

Given the presence of stochastic zeros in scRNA-seq data and the wide distribution of total UMIs per cells in our dataset, we used a pool-based size factor to deconvolute cell-specific size factor for each single-cell library for normalization purpose. Briefly, a coarse cell clustering was first performed using hierarchical clustering based on the top 50 components of principle component analysis (PCA) for the entire expression matrix. Summation of UMI counts across cells in each resolving cluster was computed as pooled-based size factor and repeated to generate a linear system for all single cells. A weighted least-squares approach is applied to solve the linear system and to deconvolute a cell-base size factor for all single cells, as implemented in Scran (version 2.1.6) (Lun et al., 2016). The UMI counts were then normalized by a cell-specific size factor and transformed as log2(normalized counts + 1). For simplicity, the transformed normalized counts are presented as log2(counts).

#### Clustering and spatial visualization

Linear dimensionality reduction was performed on the aggregated dataset using PCA. The top PCs were chosen based on elbow plots, where the percentage variance explained by each PC was plotted, and the number of principal components was chosen as a substantial drop was observed in the proportion of variance explained. Typically, 20–30 PCs were chosen based on our dataset, and were visualized using t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) (Van der Maaten and Hinton, 2008). Graph-based clustering was performed for community detection. Briefly, a k-nearest neighbors (kNN) graph was built based on the Euclidian distance of the single cells in the PCA space, the edges between the detected community were weighted using Jaccard similarity, and the Louvain method was applied to optimize the modularity of the communities. Cluster numbers were chosen based on Bayesian information criterion and biological considerations. Cluster resolution (parameter of k), t-SNE perplexity and the number of PCs used for clustering and visualization were adjusted based on the total cell number of the dataset (related to Figure 1d, g, h; Figure 1—figure supplement 1c–e, g; Figure 3i).

#### Identification of EC and non-EC cells

In the initial scRNA-seq profiling from the Tph1- bacTRAP mice, we obtained 4729 signal cells including GFP− (2412) and GFP+ (2317) cells. Clustering analysis coupled with spatial visualization in t-SNE space, as described above, indicated ~23% of the GFP+ cells clustered together with the GFP− cells. To annotate GFP− cells and GFP+ clustered with GFP- cells, we obtained gene sets from GSE92332 (Haber et al., 2017), which include gene sets associated with each major cell types in the intestinal epithelium that have been identified, including intestinal stem cells, TACs, immature enterocytes, mature enterocytes, tuft cells, goblet cells, and EEC cells. We calculated module scores for each cell cluster identified in our dataset by computing the average expression levels of each cell type gene set subtracted by the aggregated expression of all detected genes in our dataset. Cell types were assigned based on the highest module scores across all cell types as described above. Furthermore, we applied z-score transformation to the cell type-enriched gene set and validate the cell type assignment based on their respective z-score enrichment. The same approaches were employed to identify the non-EC cell types in the second scRNA-seq profiling from the Tph1-bacTRAP mice, thus annotated intestinal stem cells, TACs, immature enterocytes, mature enterocytes and colonocytes. The T lymphocytes and mast cells were identified based on the top differentially expressed genes in the respective clusters (related to Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).

#### Elimination of ileal GFP+ cells

Previous studies have indicated a significant decline of 5-HT+ cells in the distal small intestine (Reynaud et al., 2016). Consistent with such observation, in the initial scRNA-seq profiling of the single epithelial cells from Tph1-bacTRAP mice, we obtained only 225 GFP+ single-cell libraries from the ileal epithelial cells collected from eight Tph1-bacTRAP mice, which was significantly lower than those from other regions of the gut (0.1% GFP positivity compared to ~0.3–0.5% positivity in other regions). Additionally, the total number of epithelial cells obtained from the ileum in each mouse was only 20% of those from duodenum, contributing to the lower number of GFP+ cells obtained from the ileum. Upon further computational analysis, as much as 72% (162) of these GFP+ cells clustered with non-EC cells, in particular, 49% (111) were identified to have marker genes for stem cells or TACs, indicating that a majority of these cells are not fully committed EC cells. We thus eliminated ileum from further analysis.

#### Identification of differentially expressed genes in cell populations

To identify genes expressed at significantly higher level in one cluster or region than the other clusters or regions, we used the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, which is non-parametric and does not assume normality. Correction for multiple testing was performed using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure to control the FDR. We ran differential expression tests between each pair of clusters (regions) for all possible pairwise comparisons, as implemented in Scran (version 2.1.6). For a given cluster (region), the DE genes were filtered using the maximum FDR q-values across all pairwise comparisons. Genes that are known to be associated with dissociation process were not considered to be differentially expressed genes (van den Brink et al., 2017). For Figures 1l, 2f, and 4e, DE genes were obtained using maximum FDR <10–10.

#### Identification of signature genes for clusters

To identify maximally specific genes for each EC cell clusters, we performed pairwise differential gene expression analysis as described above between each pair of clusters for all possible pairwise comparisons. For a given cluster, putative signature genes were ordered based on FDR (FDR <10–10, the smallest FDR was ranked on top). The final signature genes lists were obtained by calculating the rank product for selected genes in all pairwise comparisons. Rank product statistic (Heskes et al., 2014) was used to determine p values for each marker gene and was adjusted by the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure to correct multiple hypothesis testing. To ensure the signature genes are enriched in EC cells but not other cell types in gut epithelium, the candidate genes were evaluated against both GFP− and non-EC cells identified in our own datasets and against the GSE92332 dataset (Haber et al., 2017).

#### GO term enrichment analysis

Differentially expressed genes identified by regions (Figure 1h) or by clusters (Figure 2h, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) were selected by FDR <10–10 and subjected to enrichment analysis by accumulative hypergeometric test followed by Sidak–Bonferroni correction as implemented in Metascape (Zhou et al., 2019). The resulting GO terms were selected by q-values that are presented by the size of the hexagons. The number of DE genes identified in the GO terms is represented by heatmap.

#### Comparison with public datasets

We compared neuropeptidergic hypothalamic neurons with EC cells based on two considerations: (1) hypothalamic neurons produce many hormone peptides similar to gut EEC cells, and (2) colonic EC cells are enriched with many neuronal signatures. We extracted expression matrices and metadata from GSE74672 (Romanov et al., 2017). Cell types were catalogued as indicated by metadata. Data were processed in the same pipeline as described for the Tph1-bacTRAP or Neurod1+ dataset. DE gene analysis was performed to identify neuron-enriched genes against both microglia and oligodendrocytes (FDR <10–10). The resulting gene set was used to compare EC cells originated from different segments of the gut. To identify orthogonal signature genes from human gut mucosa, we cross-compared the Neurod1+ dataset with GSE12597021, where human gut mucosal cells were isolated from biopsy samples in ileum, colon and rectum. Since no selection has been applied to dissociated human epithelial cells, <1% of captured cells are EEC cells. We identified 63 L cells and 34 EC cells in total, which were determined as Pyy+, Gcg+, or Pyy+/Gcg+ for the former, and Tph1+ for the latter. Data were processed in the same manner as Tph1-bacTRAP or Neurod1+ dataset.

### Statistics

In addition to the statistic tests described in the data analysis section, the following tests were performed:

For Figures 1i and 2j and Figure 2—figure supplement 1g, h; A two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test was performed to test whether two underlying probability distributions are the same. Implemented by scipy.stats.ks_2samp in python.

For Figure 2d: An unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-test was employed to test whether the positive fractions identified in the villi are significantly different from the ones observed in the crypts.

For Figure 2i: Hypergeometric testing for enrichment of indicated hormones in the Cck+/Tph1+ population versus the Tph1+ population was performed and implemented by scipy.stats.hypergeom in Python.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.90596.3.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.90596.3.sa1)

Summary:

The authors investigated the expression profile of enterochromaffine (EC) cells after creating a new tryptophan hydroxylase 1 (Tph1) GFP-reporter mouse using scRNAseq and confirmative RNAscope analysis. They distinguish 14 clusters of Tph1+ cells found along the gut axis. The manuscript focuses on two of these, (i) a multihormonal cell type shown to express markers of pathogen/toxin and nutrient detection in the proximal small intestine, and (ii) on a EC-cluster in the distal colon, which expresses Piezo2, rendering these cells mechanosensitive. In- and ex- vivo data explore the role of the mechanosensitive EC population for intestinal/colonic transit, using chemogenetic activation, diptheria-toxin receptor dependent cell ablation and conditional gut epithelial specific Piezo2 knock-out. Whilst some of these data are confirmative of previous reports - Piezo2 has been implicated in mechanosensitive serotonin release previously, as referred to by the authors - the data are solid and emphasize the importance of mechanosensitive serotonin release for colonic propulsion. The transcriptomic data will guide future research.

Strengths:

The transcriptomic data, whilst confirmative, is more granular than previous data sets. Employing new tools to establish a role of mechanosensitive EC cells for colonic and thus total intestinal transit.

Weaknesses:

(1) The proposed villus/crypt distribution of the14 cell types is not verified adequately. The RNAscope and immunohistochemistry samples presented do not allow assessment if this interpretation is correct - spatial transcriptomics, now approaching single cell resolution, likely will help to verify this claim.

(2) The physiological function and/or functionality of most of the transcriptomically enriched gene products has not been assessed. Whilst a role for Piezo2 expressing cells for colonic transit is convincingly demonstrated the nature of the mechanical stimulus or the stimulus-secretion coupling downstream of Piezo2 activation is not clear.

Comments on revisions: I am happy with the manuscript as is.

results.result: EC cells constitute less than 1% of intestinal epithelial cells but produce >90% of the body's serotonin and modulate diverse physiological functions. Dysregulation of peripheral 5-HT levels is implicated in gastrointestinal diseases, cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, sudden infant death syndrome, and psychiatric disorders including autism spectrum disorders.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C8 are all supported by citations to prior literature and represent established knowledge about EC cells and serotonin. These claims provide important background context for the study but do not represent novel findings from the current work.

results.result: The Tph1-bacTRAP reporter line successfully labels EC cells, with all GFP+ cells in the duodenum and >95% in jejunum and large intestine immunoreactive for 5-HT. scRNA-seq confirmed that 88.9% of GFP+ cells express Tph1, and 97.3% and 98.8% express the established EC markers Chga and Chgb, respectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C15 are well-supported by immunofluorescence and scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1a,b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1e. The validation of the Tph1-bacTRAP line is critical for the subsequent analyses and demonstrates high specificity for EC cells.

results.result: 23% of GFP+ cells clustered with GFP− cells in the initial analysis, though these cells had higher levels of EC marker genes compared to the GFP− cells they clustered with.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C17 are supported by cluster analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d-f. The authors appropriately acknowledge this heterogeneity and provide a reasonable interpretation that these may represent cells not fully committed to the EC lineage or low-level expression in other cell types.

results.result: A total of 3,526 EC cells were retained for analysis from the second profiling experiment. The most significant transcriptomic distinction was observed between small intestinal and colonic EC cells by PCA, even though all EC cells expressed a core set of EC markers.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C20 are supported by the data processing methods and PCA shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1h,i. The regional distinction is a key finding that motivates the subsequent detailed characterization of EC subpopulations.

results.result: Regional transcription factor expression patterns distinguish EC cells along the rostro-caudal axis. Pitx2 and Osr2 show preferential enrichment in different gut segments, while Hox genes are observed only in the colon, with Hoxb13 specifically in the distal colon. This pattern is largely conserved in human gut mucosa, with OSR2 and HOXB13 enriched in ileum and rectum, respectively. Olfr78 and Olfr558 are enriched in colon but not small intestine.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C28 are supported by expression data shown in Figure 1e,f and citations to prior literature. The conservation of regional TF patterns in human samples (C25-C27) strengthens the translational relevance of the findings. The consistency with prior work on Olfr78/Olfr558 (C28) provides additional validation.

results.result: 14 EC clusters were identified using the Louvain method, mostly demarcated by regions: duodenum (clusters 1-6), jejunum (clusters 7-10), proximal colon (clusters 11-12), and distal colon (clusters 13-14). EC cells from duodenum and jejunum displayed a continuum in tSNE space, indicating gradual transcriptomic change in the small intestine, whereas colonic EC cells formed distinct clusters. Cluster 6 (duodenum) was projected away from other SI EC cells, suggesting a distinct molecular profile.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C34 are supported by clustering analysis and tSNE visualization shown in Figure 1g,h. The identification of 14 distinct EC clusters is a major finding of the study. The observation about cluster 6 (C34) is appropriately noted as requiring further investigation, which is provided later in the manuscript.

results.result: All intestinal EEC cells, including EC cells, derive from Neurog3+ cells. Crypt EC cells preferentially express Tac1, while villus EC cells preferentially express Sct. Based on these markers, clusters 4/5 (duodenum) and 8/9 (jejunum) were annotated as crypt clusters, and clusters 2/3/6 (duodenum) and 10 (jejunum) as villus clusters.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C39 are supported by established knowledge (C35) and citations to prior lineage tracing studies (C36-C37). The cluster annotations (C38-C39) are supported by expression data shown in Figure 2a and validated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b-e. The authors appropriately note that this division reflects a gradient rather than a precise boundary.

results.result: EC cells exhibit differential expression of sensors and hormones along the crypt-villus axis. Ucn3 was frequently observed in crypt clusters 4/5, while Cartpt was enriched in villus cluster 3. smRNA-FISH validated that Ucn3 and Cartpt are selectively co-expressed with Tph1 but not Cck. Ucn3 was found in 57.0% of Tph1+ cells at the crypt/neck but only 24.0% in the villus. Cartpt was found in 63% of Tph1+ cells in the villus but only 16% in the crypt. Similarly, Trpa1 was detected in crypt cluster 5, while Trpm2 was co-expressed with 75% of Tph1+ cells in villi but only 12.5% in crypts. These findings suggest EC cells switch from Tac1/Ucn3/Trpa1 to Sct/Cartpt/Trpm2 as they migrate from crypt to villus.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C50 are well-supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 2a and validated by smRNA-FISH shown in Figure 2b-e. The quantification provides precise percentages with error estimates. The inference about signature switching (C50) is reasonable based on the spatial distribution data, though it remains correlative rather than demonstrating a causal developmental trajectory.

results.result: Genes associated with oxidative detoxification were preferentially enriched in crypt clusters 5/4. GO enrichment analysis revealed that cluster 1 (progenitor) was enriched with terms 'translation' and 'ribosome biogenesis', crypt clusters 4/5 with metabolism and detoxification terms, and villus clusters 2/3 with 'hemostasis', 'viral process', and 'neutrophil degranulation', suggesting involvement in host defense.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C54 are supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1f and GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2f. The functional interpretations are reasonable based on the GO terms, though direct functional validation would strengthen these conclusions.

results.result: Cluster 6 expressed the highest levels of Sct, Cck, and Ghrl, followed by Gcg and Nts. This cluster was almost exclusively duodenal EC cells (198/203, 97.5%) and comprised 10.9% of all retained duodenal EC cells. Immunohistochemistry validated that 5.8% of 5-HT+ cells were CCK+, representing 30.9% of CCK+ cells. Of the 5-HT/CCK double-positive cells, 82% were positive for ghrelin, 39.5% for oxyntomodulin, 8.9% for neurotensin, and 3.0% for GIP.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C63 are supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1i and immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 2g-i. The identification of this rare multi-hormonal EC subpopulation is a significant finding. The validation by orthogonal methods (scRNA-seq and immunohistochemistry) strengthens the conclusions.

results.result: Onecut3 (Oc3) was highly enriched in cluster 6 cells. smRNA-FISH revealed that 100% of Cck+/Tph1+ cells were Oc3+, while only 11.4% of Cck-/Tph1+ cells and 58% of Cck+/Tph1− cells were Oc3+. Oc3 single-positive cells were rarely observed (1.8%). Triple-positive cells (Cck+/Oc3+/Tph1+) were more frequently observed in the villus (25%) than in the crypt (6%). The fraction of Cck+/Oc3+ cells decreased from 69.3% in the crypt to 22.8% in the villus, while Tph1+/Oc3+ cells increased from 17.3% to 38.0%, suggesting Cck+/Oc3+ cells gradually acquire Tph1 expression during migration to the villus.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C72 are supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 2j and smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 3a-d. The identification of Oc3 as a marker for Cck+/Tph1+ cells is a significant finding. The inference about gradual acquisition of Tph1 expression (C72) is reasonable based on the spatial distribution data, though it remains correlative and would benefit from lineage tracing experiments.

results.result: Cluster 6 cells express a dual molecular signature. Crp was discretely expressed in cluster 6 and mapped to Cck+/Tph1+ cells by smRNA-FISH. Pathogen-associated molecular pattern recognition genes (Tlr2, Tlr5) were found in cluster 6 and validated by smRNA-FISH to be specific to Cck+/Tph1+ cells. Nutrient sensing GPCRs (Mc4r, Casr) were distinctly identified in cluster 6 and validated by smRNA-FISH to be specific to Cck+/Tph1+ cells. Among Mc4r+ or Casr+ cells, >85% co-expressed at least one pathogen/toxin recognition gene, suggesting a dual molecular signature associated with disparate functions in Cck+/Tph1+/Oc3+ cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C80 are supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3e and smRNA-FISH validation shown in Figure 3g,h and Figure 3—figure supplement 1. The identification of this dual sensory signature is a significant finding. The high co-expression rate (>85%) of nutrient sensors with pathogen/toxin recognition genes (C79) strongly supports the conclusion of a dual signature (C80).

results.result: In the Neurod1+ EEC dataset, a discrete cluster with high levels of Cck, Sct, Tph1, Ghrl, Gcg, and Nts was identified and annotated as a Cck+/Tph1+ cluster. Oc3 and key signature genes from cluster 6 were specifically identified in this population, confirming that the Cck+/Tph1+ population in the Neurod1-tdTomato dataset is equivalent to cluster 6 in the Tph1-GFP dataset.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C83 are supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3i,j and Figure 3—figure supplement 1. The validation of cluster 6 findings in an independent dataset using a different genetic model (Neurod1-tdTomato) significantly strengthens the conclusions about this EC subpopulation.

results.result: In the Neurod1+ dataset, SI EC cells were preferentially enriched with Trpa1, Trpm2, Cartpt, and Ucn3. Casr was enriched in Cck+/Tph1+ cells, while Mc4r was primarily found in Cck+/Tph1+ cells from SI and additionally in distal colonic L cells. ~99% of Casr+ or Mc4r+ cells in the Cck+/Tph1+ cluster co-expressed at least one pathogen/toxin recognition sensor gene.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C87 are supported by scRNA-seq data from the Neurod1-tdTomato dataset shown in Figure 3j and Figure 3—figure supplement 1j. These findings provide independent validation of the key observations from the Tph1-bacTRAP dataset, strengthening the overall conclusions.

results.result: Distinct molecular sensors were identified in EC cells versus other EEC cells. Cnr1 was enriched in Gip-dominant K cells, Asic5 in delta cells, and Gper1 in K cells. Stra6 was exclusively identified in distal colonic L cells and mapped to Pyy+ cells. Gpbar1 was found in proximal/distal colonic L cells rather than EC cells. Ffar1 was found in almost all Cck+ cells and Gcg+ L cells from both SI and colon. Ffar2 was widely observed in all EEC cells except K cells, while Ffar3 was primarily detected in L, I, and N cells. Almost all molecular sensors were confined to EEC cells with little or no expression in other epithelial cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C96 are supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3j and smRNA-FISH validation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2. The comprehensive characterization of sensor expression across EEC subtypes is a significant contribution. The validation by smRNA-FISH and comparison with public datasets strengthens the conclusions. However, the claim about Gpbar1 (C92) should be interpreted cautiously as the authors note they may not have detected low expression levels.

results.result: Proximal colonic EC cells encompassed two clusters: Iapp+/Cpb2+/Serpine1+/Sct+ cluster 11 and Il12a+/Olfr558+/Olfr78+/Tac1+ cluster 12. GO analysis indicated involvement in coagulation regulation, supported by expression of Cpb2 and Serpine1. Iapp was validated in cluster 11 by smRNA-FISH. Olfr558 and Olfr78 (short-chain fatty acid sensors) were enriched in cluster 12. Il12a was concomitantly expressed in cluster 12 and validated by smRNA-FISH. smRNA-FISH mapped Olfr558 and Il12a to separate subsets of EC cells expressing Cpb2.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C102 are supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4a, GO analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, and smRNA-FISH validation shown in Figure 4b,c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1b. The identification of functionally distinct proximal colonic EC subpopulations is a significant finding. The validation by smRNA-FISH strengthens the conclusions.

results.result: Ascl1, encoding a TF required for early neural tube specification, was found in distal colonic EC cells (clusters 13 and 14) and exclusively mapped to Tph1+ cells but not Pyy+ cells in the distal colon, nor to any cells in proximal colon or jejunum. This feature was conserved in human gut mucosa, where ASCL1 was only detected in TPH1+ cells from the rectum.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C105 are supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figures 1e and 4a, smRNA-FISH shown in Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 1c, and human data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The unexpected finding of Ascl1 in distal colonic EC cells is significant, and the conservation in human samples strengthens the translational relevance.

results.result: Distal colonic EC cells were overwhelmingly associated with GO terms 'neuron projection morphogenesis', 'axon development', and 'microtubule-based process'. Numerous genes indicative of neuronal identity were mutually enriched in distal colonic ECs. Consistently, EC cells in the distal colon exhibited unique long basal processes (50-100 µm) with 5-HT concentrated in the processes, in contrast to typical flask-shaped EEC cells in proximal colon or SI.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C108 are supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 4e and Figure 4—figure supplement 1e, scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4g, and immunofluorescence shown in Figure 4f and Figure 4—figure supplement 1f. The identification of neuron-like features in distal colonic EC cells is a major finding. The morphological validation by immunofluorescence provides strong support for the transcriptomic observations.

results.result: Foxj1 and Dnah9, genes required for cilia formation, were selectively enriched in cluster 13 and validated by smRNA-FISH in distal colonic EC cells but not in proximal colonic EC cells or Pyy+ L cells. Genes associated with GO terms 'cilium assembly/organization' were enriched in distal colonic EC cells. Cilia were identified by immunostaining against IFT88 and found to exclusively co-stain with 5-HT.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C111 are supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4a, smRNA-FISH shown in Figure 4h and Figure 4—figure supplement 1g, GO analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,h, and immunostaining shown in Figure 4i. The identification of ciliated EC cells in the distal colon is a novel finding with potential functional implications for chemosensation.

results.result: Piezo2, encoding a mechanosensitive ion channel, was identified in almost all distal colonic EC cells. smRNA-FISH revealed robust expression of Piezo2 in Ascl1+/Tph1+ cells in the epithelial layer of distal colon mucosa. Low levels of Piezo2 signals were observed in the lamina propria throughout the gut. Piezo1 transcripts were either undetectable or sparsely observed in epithelium and lamina propria. Piezo2 was not detected in Tph1+ cells from proximal colon, ileum, jejunum, and duodenum via smRNA-FISH. qPCR showed a significant enrichment of Piezo2 (up to 360-fold) in GFP+ cells from distal colon compared to other regions. Based on multiple lines of evidence, Piezo2 is preferentially enriched in neuron-like distal colonic EC cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C118 are supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4a, smRNA-FISH shown in Figure 5a-c and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a,b, and qPCR shown in Figure 5d. The identification of Piezo2 in distal colonic EC cells is a major finding. The validation by multiple orthogonal methods (scRNA-seq, smRNA-FISH, qPCR) provides strong support. However, the authors appropriately note that previous studies detected Piezo2 in small intestine by RT-PCR and immunohistochemistry, suggesting expression below the detection threshold of the current methods.

results.result: Concomitant expression of Piezo2 with Foxj1 and Olfr78 was revealed by scRNA-seq and validated by smRNA-FISH, suggesting that a subpopulation of Piezo2+/Tph1+ cells are mechanosensory cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C120 are supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 4a and smRNA-FISH shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1i. The inference that these cells are mechanosensory (C120) is reasonable based on the co-expression of Piezo2 (mechanosensor), Foxj1 (cilia), and Olfr78 (chemosensor), though direct functional validation would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: Chemogenetic activation of Piezo2+ cells leads to serotonin release. 15 min after intracolonic CNO administration, a robust elevation (2.1-fold) of serum serotonin was observed in Piezo2-CHRM3* mice but not in WT or Rosa26-LSL-CHRM3* mice. In vitro, CNO stimulation elevated serotonin release from mCitrine+/Epcam+ cells of distal colon by 1.9-fold, whereas mCitrine−/Epcam+ cells failed to respond. This demonstrates that CNO-mediated activation of Piezo2+ cells leads to robust serotonin release from epithelial EC cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C125 are supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5f and Figure 5—figure supplement 2a, and in vitro serotonin release assay shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2d,e. The chemogenetic approach provides strong evidence for the functional capacity of Piezo2+ cells to release serotonin. The appropriate controls (WT, Rosa26-LSL-CHRM3*, saline) strengthen the conclusions.

results.result: Chemogenetic activation of Piezo2+ cells accelerates colon motility. Increased fecal pellet output was observed from Piezo2-CHRM3* mice within 15 min after CNO administration. In a bead expulsion assay, colon motility was significantly accelerated after CNO treatment, with time to expel shortened from 7.24 min in WT controls to 1.16 min in Piezo2-CHRM3*/mCitrine animals. No difference was observed in untreated or saline-treated cohorts.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C128 are supported by fecal pellet assay data shown in Figure 5g and bead expulsion assay shown in Figure 5h and Figure 5—figure supplement 2f. The dramatic acceleration of colon motility upon Piezo2+ cell activation is a major finding. The appropriate controls strengthen the conclusions.

results.result: Htr4, encoding the prokinetic 5-HT4 receptor, was selectively expressed by epithelium in the deep crypts of distal colon. The long basal processes of EC cells filled with 5-HT extend toward the base of the crypts where Htr4 is preferentially expressed.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C130 are supported by smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1e. This observation suggests a potential mechanism for 5-HT signaling from EC cells to Htr4+ epithelial cells, though functional validation would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: Genetic depletion of Piezo2+ cells impairs colon motility. Intraluminal DT administration in Piezo2-DTR mice caused profound co-depletion of Piezo2 and Tph1 transcripts and substantial loss of 5-HT+ cells in the distal colon, while general epithelial architecture was maintained. This resulted in 42% reduction in fecal pellet output, substantial delay in bead expulsion (36.9 min vs 8.2 min in WT), and delayed whole gut transit time (181.8 min vs 136.7 min in WT). Gastric emptying was not affected, but small intestine transit time showed a small but statistically significant slowdown.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C138 are supported by smRNA-FISH shown in Figure 6b,c and Figure 6—figure supplement 1, immunofluorescence shown in Figure 6b,d, and motility assays shown in Figure 6e-i. The loss-of-function experiments provide strong evidence that Piezo2+ EC cells are required for normal colon motility. The appropriate controls (WT, Rosa26-LSL-DTR) strengthen the conclusions. The small effect on small intestine transit (C137) is interesting and the authors provide reasonable explanations.

results.result: Epithelial-specific deletion of Piezo2 using Villin-cre resulted in 15.9% early mortality around 21-34 days after birth, with affected animals showing 42% reduction in body weight. Piezo2 depletion was observed in the isolated epithelial layer of distal colon by qPCR and smRNA-FISH. Tph1 and Chga levels remained unaltered, and no change was observed in basal serotonin levels. Residual Piezo2 signals were observed in some Tph1+ cells, suggesting incomplete depletion. Importantly, Piezo2 signals in the lamina propria remained largely unaltered, indicating only epithelial Piezo2 was abolished.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C145 are supported by survival data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1a, body weight data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1a-c, qPCR shown in Figure 7a, smRNA-FISH shown in Figure 7b, and ELISA shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1g,h. The early mortality phenotype (C139) is an important observation suggesting a critical role for epithelial Piezo2. The incomplete depletion (C144) and preservation of lamina propria Piezo2 (C145) are important caveats that the authors appropriately acknowledge.

results.result: Epithelial-specific deletion of Piezo2 impairs colon motility. BEA revealed significant slowing of expulsion in Piezo2 CKO mice (33.7 min male, 32.3 min female) compared to Piezo2fl/fl controls (9.25 min male, 8.9 min female). Prolonged whole gut transit time was observed in Piezo2 CKO mice (182 min male, 175 min female) compared to controls (146 min male, 143 min female). No difference was observed in small intestinal transit. Fluorescent dye travel in colon at 120 min was significantly shorter in Piezo2 CKO mice (51.2%) compared to controls (72.1%). Loss of Piezo2 in epithelial EC cells primarily affected colon motility.
results.evaluation: Claims C146-C150 are supported by bead expulsion assay shown in Figure 7d, whole gut transit time shown in Figure 7e, small intestinal transit shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1k, and colon transit shown in Figure 7f,g. The epithelial-specific deletion provides strong evidence that epithelial Piezo2 is required for normal colon motility. The lack of effect on small intestinal transit (C148) contrasts with the DTR experiments, which the authors appropriately discuss.

results.result: Piezo2+/Ascl1+/Tph1+ cells are required for normal colon motility.
results.evaluation: Claim C151 is supported by the combined evidence from chemogenetic activation (C121-C128) and genetic depletion experiments (C131-C150). The gain- and loss-of-function approaches provide strong converging evidence for this conclusion.

results.result: 14 EC subpopulations were resolved characterized by distinct chemical and mechanical sensors, TFs, subcellular structures, and spatial distribution. The transcriptome diversity of EC cells is closely related to their spatial distribution. The first layer of complexity is defined along the rostro-caudal axis between small intestine and colon, with gradual enrichment of neuron-like transcriptome from small intestine to distal colon, including specific expression of Ascl1 in distal colonic EC cells. A second layer of complexity is resolved along the crypt-villus axis.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C156 are supported by the comprehensive scRNA-seq and spatial imaging data presented throughout the manuscript and summarized in Figure 8. These claims represent the major conclusions of the study and are well-supported by the data.

results.result: Piezo2 is preferentially expressed in distal colonic EC cells that also have neuronal expression profiles. Depletion of Piezo2 from these cells caused a fourfold increase in bead expulsion time, implying that mechanical stimulus caused 5-HT release and initiation of colon propulsion. Consistent with this, 5-HT released from EC has been shown to cause colorectal propulsion in mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C157-C159 are supported by the combined evidence from scRNA-seq, smRNA-FISH, and genetic ablation experiments shown throughout the manuscript. The inference about mechanical stimulus causing 5-HT release (C158) is reasonable based on the bead expulsion data, and the citation to prior literature (C159) provides additional support.

results.result: Piezo2 signals were observed in the lamina propria throughout the intestine. Piezo2 was detected via scRNA-seq in a subset of sensory DRG neurons innervating the colon. It is possible that both distal colonic EC cells and sensory DRG neurons contribute to mechanosensory sensing and motility control.
results.evaluation: Claims C160-C162 are supported by smRNA-FISH data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b and citation to prior literature (Hockley et al., 2019). The suggestion of dual contribution (C162) is appropriately presented as a possibility rather than a definitive conclusion, acknowledging the need for further investigation.

results.result: A cluster of Cck+/Oc3+/Tph1+ EC cells in duodenal villi was enriched with two sets of sensory molecules: pathogen/toxin recognition enzymes/receptors and nutrient sensing/homeostasis receptors, suggesting these cells react to gastric content entering the duodenum. The gut has a well-established defensive role to expel noxious chemicals and toxins by nausea and vomiting initiated by 5-HT release. The findings suggest Cck+/Oc3+/Tph1+ cells equipped with pathogen/toxin recognition receptors may play a role in this defense mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C163-C166 are supported by scRNA-seq and smRNA-FISH data shown in Figures 3e-h and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and citations to prior literature (Mawe and Hoffman, 2013; Andrews et al., 1998). The identification of the dual sensory signature is well-supported (C163). The inference about reacting to gastric content (C164) and role in defense (C166) are reasonable based on the molecular signatures and established knowledge (C165), though direct functional validation would strengthen these conclusions.

results.result: The authors generated a Tph1-bacTRAP mouse line to label EC cells and validated it by showing that GFP+ cells co-localize with 5-HT immunoreactivity (all in duodenum, >95% in jejunum and large intestine) and express EC markers Tph1, Chga, and Chgb at high frequencies by scRNA-seq. The most significant transcriptomic distinction was observed between small intestinal and colonic EC cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe the transcriptomic data as 'solid' and 'more granular than previous data sets,' indicating acceptance of the Tph1-bacTRAP model validation and the regional transcriptomic distinctions. No concerns were raised about the specificity or quality of the reporter line or the scRNA-seq profiling.

results.result: Using unsupervised clustering, the authors resolved 14 EC subpopulations that were mostly demarcated by intestinal region (duodenum clusters 1-6, jejunum 7-10, proximal colon 11-12, distal colon 13-14). Small intestinal EC cells displayed a continuum in tSNE space, while colonic EC cells formed distinct clusters. The transcriptome diversity of EC cells is closely related to their spatial distribution along the rostro-caudal axis.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the transcriptomic data as 'solid' and note that it 'will guide future research,' indicating acceptance of the 14-cluster resolution and regional organization. The editor states 'the evidence supporting the authors' claims is solid,' affirming the clustering results.

results.result: The authors resolved a second layer of EC cell complexity along the crypt-villus axis in the small intestine. Crypt clusters (4/5 in duodenum, 8/9 in jejunum) were distinguished from villus clusters (2/3/6 in duodenum, 10 in jejunum) based on differential expression of Tac1/Ucn3/Trpa1 (crypt-enriched) versus Sct/Cartpt/Trpm2 (villus-enriched), validated by smRNA-FISH. GO analysis revealed functional specialization: crypt clusters enriched for metabolism/detoxification, villus clusters for host defense.
results.evaluation: While reviewers accept the transcriptomic data as solid, one reviewer specifically notes that 'the proposed villus/crypt distribution of the 14 cell types is not verified adequately' and states 'the RNAscope and immunohistochemistry samples presented do not allow assessment if this interpretation is correct.' The reviewer suggests spatial transcriptomics would help verify this claim, indicating uncertainty about the crypt-villus assignments.

results.result: The authors identified a rare multihormonal EC cell population (cluster 6) in the duodenal villi, representing <0.1% of total duodenal epithelial cells. These Cck+/Tph1+/Oc3+ cells co-express multiple hormones (Sct, Ghrl, Gcg, Nts) and show spatial progression: Cck+/Oc3+ cells in crypts gradually acquire Tph1 expression as they migrate to villi, where triple-positive cells are more frequent.
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe the manuscript as focusing on 'a multihormonal cell type shown to express markers of pathogen/toxin and nutrient detection in the proximal small intestine,' indicating acceptance of this cluster 6 characterization. The data are described as 'solid,' and no concerns were raised about the identification or validation of this rare population.

results.result: Cluster 6 Cck+/Tph1+/Oc3+ cells are enriched with a dual molecular signature: pathogen/toxin recognition molecules (Crp, Tlr2, Tlr5) and nutrient sensing receptors (Mc4r, Casr). Over 85% of Mc4r+ or Casr+ cells co-expressed pathogen/toxin recognition genes. The authors suggest these cells may react to gastric content entering the duodenum and play a role in gut defense mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly note the manuscript focuses on this 'multihormonal cell type shown to express markers of pathogen/toxin and nutrient detection,' indicating acceptance of the dual sensory signature. The data are described as 'solid,' and no concerns were raised about the molecular characterization or functional interpretation of these cells.

results.result: In the proximal colon, EC cells encompassed two clusters: cluster 11 (Iapp+/Cpb2+/Serpine1+/Sct+) involved in coagulation regulation, and cluster 12 (Il12a+/Olfr558+/Olfr78+/Tac1+) expressing short-chain fatty acid sensors. These represent distinct subpopulations with different physiological roles.
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe the transcriptomic data as 'solid' and note it 'will guide future research,' indicating acceptance of the proximal colon EC cell heterogeneity. No specific concerns were raised about these cluster characterizations or their functional annotations.

results.result: Distal colonic EC cells (clusters 13-14) express Ascl1 (a neural fate commitment transcription factor) exclusively in Tph1+ cells, conserved in human rectum. These cells are enriched for neuronal genes and GO terms related to neuron projection morphogenesis, axon development, and cilium assembly. Morphologically, they exhibit unique long basal processes (50-100 μm) with 5-HT concentrated in the processes, and express cilia markers (Foxj1, Dnah9, IFT88).
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe the data as 'solid' and note the manuscript focuses on 'a EC-cluster in the distal colon, which expresses Piezo2, rendering these cells mechanosensitive,' implicitly accepting the neuronal characterization of distal colonic EC cells. The transcriptomic data showing neuronal features are part of the accepted 'granular' dataset.

results.result: Piezo2, encoding a mechanosensitive ion channel, was identified in almost all distal colonic EC cells by scRNA-seq and validated by smRNA-FISH to be robustly expressed in Ascl1+/Tph1+ cells in the epithelial layer. qPCR showed up to 360-fold enrichment in distal colon GFP+ cells compared to other gut regions. Piezo2 was not detected in EC cells from proximal colon or small intestine. A subpopulation co-expresses Piezo2 with Foxj1 and Olfr78, suggesting mechanosensory function.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state the manuscript focuses on 'a EC-cluster in the distal colon, which expresses Piezo2, rendering these cells mechanosensitive' and describe the data as 'solid.' One reviewer notes 'Piezo2 has been implicated in mechanosensitive serotonin release previously' but states 'the data are solid and emphasize the importance of mechanosensitive serotonin release for colonic propulsion,' indicating acceptance of the Piezo2 expression characterization.

results.result: Chemogenetic activation of Piezo2+ cells using CNO in Piezo2-CHRM3* mice led to robust serotonin release (2.1-fold elevation in serum, 1.9-fold from isolated mCitrine+/Epcam+ cells), increased fecal pellet output, and significantly accelerated colon motility (bead expulsion time shortened from 7.24 to 1.16 min). No effects were observed in wild-type or control mice.
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe the data as 'solid' and note the authors 'employ new tools to establish a role of mechanosensitive EC cells for colonic and thus total intestinal transit.' The chemogenetic activation experiments are part of the accepted evidence demonstrating the functional role of Piezo2+ cells in colonic motility.

results.result: Diphtheria toxin-mediated ablation of Piezo2+ cells in Piezo2-DTR mice resulted in profound co-depletion of Piezo2 and Tph1 transcripts and substantial loss of 5-HT+ cells in the distal colon (validated by smRNA-FISH and immunofluorescence), while maintaining general epithelial architecture. This led to 42% reduction in fecal pellet output, substantial delay in bead expulsion (36.9 vs 8.2 min), small but significant slowdown in small intestine transit, and delayed whole gut transit time (181.8 vs 136.7 min).
results.evaluation: Reviewers state 'a role for Piezo2 expressing cells for colonic transit is convincingly demonstrated' and describe the data as 'solid.' The diphtheria toxin ablation experiments are explicitly accepted as part of the evidence establishing the functional importance of Piezo2+ EC cells for intestinal motility.

results.result: Conditional gut epithelial-specific Piezo2 knockout (Villin-cre;Piezo2fl/fl) resulted in Piezo2 depletion from distal colon epithelium (validated by qPCR and smRNA-FISH) without affecting Tph1/Chga levels or basal serotonin. Residual Piezo2 signals were observed in some Tph1+ cells and lamina propria remained unaltered. This led to significant slowing of bead expulsion (33.7 vs 9.25 min), prolonged whole gut transit (182 vs 146 min), and shorter colon transit distance (51.2% vs 72.1%), with no effect on small intestinal transit. The authors conclude that Piezo2+/Ascl1+/Tph1+ cells are required for normal colon motility.
results.evaluation: Reviewers state 'a role for Piezo2 expressing cells for colonic transit is convincingly demonstrated' using 'conditional gut epithelial specific Piezo2 knock-out.' The data are described as 'solid,' and the conclusion about Piezo2+ cells being required for normal colon motility is accepted as part of the manuscript's core findings.

results.result: Regional transcription factors (Pitx2, Osr2, Hox genes) showed preferential enrichment along the gut axis, with Hox genes observed only in the colon and Hoxb13 specifically in the distal colon. This pattern was largely conserved in human gut mucosa, with OSR2 and HOXB13 preferentially enriched in human ileum and rectum, respectively.
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe the transcriptomic data as 'solid' and 'more granular than previous data sets,' indicating acceptance of the regional transcription factor patterns. The conservation in human samples strengthens the findings, and no concerns were raised about these observations.

results.result: The authors identified and validated by smRNA-FISH several cluster-specific nutrient and chemical sensors in different EEC cell types: Cnr1 in K cells, Asic5 in delta cells, Gper1 in K cells, Stra6 in distal colonic L cells, and Gpbar1 in proximal/distal colonic L cells (not EC cells). Ffar1 was found in almost all Cck+ cells and Gcg+ L cells, while Ffar2 was widely observed in all EEC cells except K cells. Almost all molecular sensors were confined to EEC cells with little expression in other epithelial cell types.
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe the transcriptomic data as 'solid' and note it 'will guide future research,' indicating acceptance of the sensor molecule characterization across different EEC cell types. No concerns were raised about the identification or validation of these cluster-specific sensors.

results.result: Htr4 (encoding the 5-HT4 receptor) was selectively expressed by epithelium in the deep crypts of distal colon, and the long basal processes of EC cells filled with 5-HT extend toward the base of the crypts where Htr4 is preferentially expressed.
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe the data as 'solid' and accept the characterization of distal colonic EC cells. This observation about Htr4 localization and EC cell process orientation is part of the accepted anatomical and molecular characterization of these cells.

results.result: 15.9% of Piezo2 CKO mice died around 21-34 days after birth, with affected animals presenting 42% reduction in body weight and runt body size by the time of humane euthanasia.
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe the data as 'solid' and accept the conditional knockout experiments. While this mortality phenotype is noted, no concerns were raised about its validity or interpretation as part of the Piezo2 loss-of-function characterization.

results.result: Piezo2 signals were observed in the lamina propria throughout the intestine, and Piezo2 was previously detected in a subset of sensory DRG neurons innervating the colon. The authors suggest both distal colonic EC cells and sensory DRG neurons may contribute to mechanosensory sensing and motility control.
results.evaluation: One reviewer notes 'the nature of the mechanical stimulus or the stimulus-secretion coupling downstream of Piezo2 activation is not clear,' suggesting uncertainty about the mechanistic details. While the expression of Piezo2 in both EC cells and DRG neurons is accepted, the relative contributions and interactions between these cell types remain unclear.

results.result: Background claims about EC cells constituting <1% of intestinal epithelium, producing >90% of body's serotonin, modulating physiological functions, and dysregulation being implicated in various diseases (GI, cardiovascular, osteoporosis, SIDS, psychiatric disorders).
results.evaluation: These are well-established background facts supported by multiple literature citations. Reviewers do not question these foundational claims, which provide context for the study's importance.

results.result: Background claims about EEC cell lineage (all derive from Neurog3+ cells) and established markers (Chga/Chgb for EC cells, Tac1 for crypt EC cells, Sct for villus EC cells).
results.evaluation: These are established facts from prior literature that reviewers do not question. They provide necessary context for the cluster annotations and validation approaches used in the study.

results.result: Background claims about previously reported findings: Olfr78/Olfr558 enrichment in colon, 5-HT causing colorectal propulsion, and gut's defensive role in expelling toxins via 5-HT release.
results.evaluation: These are confirmatory findings or established facts from prior literature. One reviewer notes 'some of these data are confirmative of previous reports' but states 'the data are solid,' indicating acceptance of these observations as supporting context.

results.result: Validation of cluster 6 findings in an independent Neurod1-tdTomato scRNA-seq dataset, showing a discrete Cck+/Tph1+ cluster with high levels of Cck, Sct, Tph1, Ghrl, Gcg, and Nts. Oc3 and key signature genes from cluster 6 were specifically identified in this population, with ~99% of Casr+/Mc4r+ cells co-expressing pathogen/toxin recognition genes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe the transcriptomic data as 'solid,' and the validation in an independent dataset strengthens the cluster 6 characterization. No concerns were raised about this cross-dataset validation.

Both support regional transcriptomic distinctions (C18-C20). OpenEval highlights PCA analysis showing regional differences; peer reviewers describe data as 'solid' and accept regional organization without concerns.
